method_card.title: How to Work with Decimals and Rounding
method_card.content:
Rounding makes a number simpler to a stated accuracy. Look at the digit just after the place you are keeping: if it is 5 or more, round up; if it is 4 or less, round down.

Decimal places count digits after the point. Significant figures count from the first non-zero digit; leading zeros never count, but hold place value with zeros (3452 to 2 s.f. is 3500).

Truncation chops off digits without rounding. Estimation rounds every number to 1 significant figure, then does the easy calculation.
method_card.example:
Round 0.04673 to 2 significant figures

Step 1: The first significant figure is 4 (ignore leading zeros). The second significant figure is 6.

Step 2: Look at the next digit: 7 (5 or more, so round up).

Step 3: 6 rounds up to 7.

Answer: \(0.047\)

steps: Round every number to 1 significant figure, then do the easy calculation.
Dividing by a decimal below 1 makes the answer bigger, so \(100 \div 0.5 = 200\) is meant to look large.
An estimate is a check, not the exact value. Use the \(\approx\) sign.
gold.title: Gold: Estimating with 1 significant figure

steps: Find the place you are keeping and note that digit.
Look at the next digit to its right. If it is 5 or more, add 1 to your digit. If it is 4 or less, leave it.
Drop everything after the place you kept, keeping the right number of decimal places even if it ends in a zero.
bronze.title: Bronze: Rounding to decimal places

steps.label: Next digit

steps: Significant figures start at the first non-zero digit. Count that many, then use the next digit to round.
Leading zeros never count, but keep place value: 3452 to 2 s.f. is 3500, not 35.
Truncating is different: you just chop off the extra digits and never round up.
